ev.eur_h_millennium.title: A thousand years since the Passion
ev.eur_h_millennium.text: A third year of failed harvests, the hungry wander the roads, and the monks remind everyone that a thousand years have nearly passed since Christ suffered on the cross. Many expect the end of the world and give their land to monasteries "for the salvation of their souls".
ev.eur_h_millennium.note: The monk Rodulfus Glaber wrote of terrible famine and portents around 1033, the millennium of Christ's Passion. How widespread the "terrors of the year 1000" really were is disputed: many historians consider them a later legend.
ev.eur_h_millennium.give: Give part of your goods to the monastery
ev.eur_h_hastings.title: The Norman Conquest
ev.eur_h_hastings.text: King Harold has fallen at Hastings. On Christmas Day the Norman duke William was crowned at Westminster. The new lords speak French and are building a stone tower by the river.
ev.eur_h_hastings.note: On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated Harold II at Hastings and was crowned at Westminster on 25 December. Almost the whole English nobility was replaced by Normans; the Tower of London was begun.
ev.eur_h_hastings.resist.success: You came back alive from the fens and forests, but you have looked at the Normans differently ever since.
ev.eur_h_hastings.resist.failure: The Normans burned your village in punishment. You barely escaped.
ev.eur_h_investiture.title: Emperor and Pope
ev.eur_h_investiture.text: Pope Gregory has excommunicated Emperor Henry for appointing bishops himself. They say the emperor stood barefoot in the snow at the gates of Canossa, begging forgiveness. Everyone argues over who is right.
ev.eur_h_investiture.text.florence: Pope Gregory has excommunicated Emperor Henry, and our own Countess Matilda of Tuscany received the Pope in her castle at Canossa. The emperor stood three days barefoot in the snow at the gate. Everyone argues over who is right.
ev.eur_h_investiture.note: The Investiture Controversy was a struggle between popes and emperors over the right to appoint bishops. In January 1077 Henry IV came as a penitent to Gregory VII at Canossa, the castle of Matilda of Tuscany. The dispute ended with the Concordat of Worms in 1122.
ev.eur_h_investiture.emperor: The emperor is God's, and so are his bishops
ev.eur_h_investiture.pope: The Church must not serve princes
ev.eur_h_first_crusade.title: God wills it!
ev.eur_h_first_crusade.text: Pope Urban at Clermont has called for the liberation of Jerusalem. Peter the Hermit preaches along the roads, and crowds follow him – knights, peasants, women, children. All who take the cross will have their sins forgiven.
ev.eur_h_first_crusade.note: On 27 November 1095 Urban II called at the Council of Clermont for an expedition to the East. The First Crusade ended with the capture of Jerusalem in July 1099; many participants died on the way of hunger and disease.
ev.eur_h_first_crusade.go.success: You reached Jerusalem and came home. Few men can say as much.
ev.eur_h_first_crusade.go.failure: Hunger before Antioch, heat, disease. You came home barely alive and penniless.
ev.eur_h_first_crusade.give: Help those who go with money
ev.eur_h_rhineland_1096.title: The summer of 1096
ev.eur_h_rhineland_1096.text: Bands of crusaders marching east are attacking the Jewish communities along the Rhine – at Speyer, Worms, Mainz. Now they are at Cologne. The archbishop offers to hide the community in his villages.
ev.eur_h_rhineland_1096.note: In the spring and summer of 1096 bands of the "People's" Crusade, among them that of Count Emicho, massacred Jews in the Rhineland towns. Archbishop Hermann III of Cologne hid the community in surrounding villages, but many died even so.
ev.eur_h_rhineland_1096.neighbor.success: Your neighbour hid you in his loft until the bands had gone. You will never forget it.
ev.eur_h_rhineland_1096.neighbor.failure: The house was searched. You survived by a miracle, but your home and goods were lost.
ev.eur_h_second_crusade.title: Bernard preaches
ev.eur_h_second_crusade.text: Edessa has fallen, and Abbot Bernard of Clairvaux is travelling the land: thousands listen to him, though half do not understand his Latin. Kings Louis and Conrad have taken the cross themselves.
ev.eur_h_second_crusade.note: The Second Crusade (1147–1149) was proclaimed after the fall of Edessa in 1144. Bernard of Clairvaux preached it in France and Germany. It ended in failure before Damascus.
ev.eur_h_second_crusade.go.success: You came back, though the crusade failed. You saw Constantinople.
ev.eur_h_second_crusade.go.failure: In the mountains of Anatolia the army was routed. You came home sick and ruined.
ev.eur_h_notre_dame.title: The new cathedral
ev.eur_h_notre_dame.text: On the Île de la Cité the old church is being pulled down: Bishop Maurice de Sully is building a cathedral of Our Lady, taller and lighter than any before. The Pope himself laid the first stone. The works need hands and money.
ev.eur_h_notre_dame.note: Construction of Notre-Dame de Paris began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully; tradition says Pope Alexander III laid the first stone. The main work took nearly a century.
ev.eur_h_translators.title: The translators
ev.eur_h_translators.text: At the cathedral the translators are at work: Jewish and Mozarab scholars read Arabic books aloud while Latin clerks from France, England and Italy write them down. They say the Italian Gerard of Cremona has already translated dozens – Ptolemy, Euclid, Avicenna.
ev.eur_h_translators.note: In the twelfth century, with the support of Archbishop Raymond, Toledo became the chief centre of translation from Arabic into Latin. Gerard of Cremona (d. 1187) translated some seventy works on astronomy, mathematics and medicine.
ev.eur_h_translators.listen: Listen to what the books say
ev.eur_h_becket.title: Murder in the cathedral
ev.eur_h_becket.text: Four of the king's knights have cut down Archbishop Thomas Becket inside Canterbury Cathedral. At his tomb people already speak of miracles, and pilgrims are coming from all over England.
ev.eur_h_becket.note: Thomas Becket was murdered on 29 December 1170 after a quarrel with Henry II over the rights of the Church. He was canonised in 1173, and in 1174 the king himself did penance at the tomb. Canterbury became England's chief place of pilgrimage.
ev.eur_h_las_navas.title: The army at Toledo
ev.eur_h_las_navas.text: A huge army is gathering under the walls: Castilians, Aragonese, Navarrese and knights from beyond the Pyrenees march against the Almohads. The foreign crusaders run riot in the city, but King Alfonso asks for patience.
ev.eur_h_las_navas.note: In June 1212 the crusading army assembled at Toledo; some of those from beyond the Pyrenees attacked the Jewish quarter. On 16 July 1212 the Christians routed the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa – a turning point of the Reconquista.
ev.eur_h_las_navas.march.success: At Las Navas de Tolosa the Almohads fled. You came home with plunder.
ev.eur_h_las_navas.march.failure: You were wounded in the mountains of the Sierra Morena.
ev.eur_h_las_navas.supply: Sell the army bread on credit
ev.eur_h_las_navas.stay: Wait for the army to leave
ev.eur_h_magna_carta.title: The Great Charter
ev.eur_h_magna_carta.text: The barons, with the Londoners on their side, have forced King John to seal a charter in the meadow at Runnymede. The king promises not to imprison free men without the judgement of their peers – and the city's liberties are confirmed.
ev.eur_h_magna_carta.note: Magna Carta was sealed by King John on 15 June 1215. Within months the Pope annulled it, but it was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225 and became a foundation of English liberties.
ev.eur_h_albigensian.title: The crusade in the south
ev.eur_h_albigensian.text: The Pope has proclaimed a crusade – not overseas but to the south, against the Cathar heretics of Languedoc. Forty days of service brings forgiveness of sins, and the lands of the southern lords will go to northern knights.
ev.eur_h_albigensian.note: The Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) was proclaimed by Innocent III. After Béziers was taken in 1209 nearly its whole population was massacred. The war brought Languedoc under the French crown.
ev.eur_h_albigensian.go.success: You served your forty days and came back with plunder. Better not to remember what you saw.
ev.eur_h_albigensian.go.failure: Under the walls of Toulouse you were wounded.
ev.eur_h_albigensian.refuse: Refuse to make war on Christians
ev.eur_h_montaperti.title: Montaperti
ev.eur_h_montaperti.text: The Florentine army has been crushed by the Sienese and the Ghibellines at Montaperti. They say the little river Arbia ran red. The Ghibellines are entering the city, and the Guelf families are fleeing.
ev.eur_h_montaperti.note: On 4 September 1260 Siena and the Ghibelline Florentine exiles routed Guelf Florence at Montaperti. The Ghibellines ruled the city until 1266–1267.
ev.eur_h_cologne_cathedral.title: The foundation stone
ev.eur_h_cologne_cathedral.text: The old cathedral has burned, and Archbishop Konrad has laid the stone of a new one – on the French model but vast, worthy of the relics of the Three Kings. Master Gerhard is already drawing the plan.
ev.eur_h_cologne_cathedral.note: The foundation stone of Cologne Cathedral was laid on 15 August 1248 by Archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden. Work stopped in the sixteenth century and was finished only in 1880.
ev.eur_h_worringen.title: Worringen
ev.eur_h_worringen.text: At Worringen the citizens of Cologne, together with the Duke of Brabant, defeated the archbishop's army, and the archbishop himself was taken prisoner. From now on the city runs its own affairs.
ev.eur_h_worringen.note: The Battle of Worringen on 5 June 1288 was one of the largest battles of medieval Europe. Afterwards the archbishops effectively lost power over Cologne, which officially became a Free Imperial City in 1475.
ev.eur_h_england_expulsion.title: Expulsion
ev.eur_h_england_expulsion.text: King Edward has decreed that all Jews must leave England by All Saints' Day. You may take only what you can carry. Houses and bonds remain with the Crown.
ev.eur_h_england_expulsion.note: Edward I issued the Edict of Expulsion on 18 July 1290. The exiles went to France, Flanders and Germany. Jews officially returned to England only in 1656.
ev.eur_h_france_1306.title: Arrest and expulsion
ev.eur_h_france_1306.text: In a single day the king's men arrested every Jew in the kingdom. Property has been seized for the treasury, debts owed by Christians have passed to the king, and the Jews themselves are ordered to leave.
ev.eur_h_france_1306.note: On 22 July 1306 Philip IV the Fair ordered the Jews of France arrested, their property confiscated, and themselves expelled. The exiles went to Lorraine, Germany, Provence and Spain. In 1315 they were allowed to return.
ev.eur_h_great_famine.title: The Great Famine
ev.eur_h_great_famine.text: For the third summer running the rain pours down. Grain rots in the field, the price of bread has quadrupled, cattle die of murrain. People who were well-to-do only yesterday trudge along the roads.
ev.eur_h_great_famine.note: The Great Famine of 1315–1317 struck northern Europe after a run of rainy years, followed by a cattle plague. An estimated 5–10% of the population died.
ev.eur_h_great_famine.belt: Tighten your belt and save the seed
ev.eur_h_hundred_years.title: War for the French crown
ev.eur_h_hundred_years.text: King Edward of England has proclaimed himself the rightful King of France. A war begins, and no one knows it will outlast any lifetime. New taxes and a muster are proclaimed.
ev.eur_h_hundred_years.note: The Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) between England and France began as a dispute over the French throne after the direct Capetian line died out in 1328.
ev.eur_h_crecy.title: Crécy
ev.eur_h_crecy.text: At Crécy English archers cut down the flower of French chivalry. A year later Calais fell.
ev.eur_h_crecy.text.paris: At Crécy English archers cut down the flower of French chivalry: clouds of arrows, horses in the mud, counts lying dead. In Paris the bells toll for the fallen, and the king has come back almost without an army.
ev.eur_h_crecy.text.london: Messengers bring the news: at Crécy the king and the young prince routed the French, and our archers shot as no one in the world can. In London the bells are ringing and men drink to victory.
ev.eur_h_crecy.note: On 26 August 1346 Edward III's army routed the French at Crécy; English longbowmen played the decisive part. In 1347, after a long siege, Calais surrendered.
ev.eur_h_bank_crash.title: The banks collapse
ev.eur_h_bank_crash.text: The English king is not paying his debts, and the great companies of the Bardi and Peruzzi announce one after another that the money is gone. There is a crush at the money-changers' benches, and your savings are there too.
ev.eur_h_bank_crash.note: In 1343–1346 the greatest Florentine banks, the Peruzzi and the Bardi, collapsed. The causes were defaults by Edward III and other rulers, war and a general crisis. The crash hit thousands of depositors.
ev.eur_h_bank_crash.withdraw.success: You got almost everything out before the doors closed.
ev.eur_h_bank_crash.withdraw.failure: The doors closed in your face.
ev.eur_h_arno_flood.title: The Arno floods
ev.eur_h_arno_flood.text: Four days of downpour – and the Arno has burst its banks. The water has swept away all the bridges but one and flooded whole quarters up to the first floor. In the churches the water stands higher than the altar.
ev.eur_h_arno_flood.note: The flood of 4 November 1333 destroyed nearly all of Florence's bridges, including the Ponte Vecchio, and claimed hundreds of lives. The chronicler Giovanni Villani described the disaster in detail.
ev.eur_h_arno_flood.goods.success: You dragged the most valuable things up to the loft.
ev.eur_h_arno_flood.goods.failure: The water came faster. You yourself were barely pulled out.
ev.eur_h_black_death.title: The Great Mortality
ev.eur_h_black_death.text: Death has come from the south: fever, black swellings under the arms, and in three days a man is dead. The priests cannot bury them all, and the dead are laid in rows in common pits. They say a third of all people have already died.
ev.eur_h_black_death.text.florence: The plague reached Florence in the spring: fever, black swellings, and in three days a man is dead. The rich flee to villas in the hills, the poor remain. They say the city will lose more than half its people.
ev.eur_h_black_death.note: The Black Death, an epidemic of bubonic and pneumonic plague, reached Europe in 1347 through Black Sea and Mediterranean ports. In 1347–1351 between a third and a half of the population died. Boccaccio described it in the introduction to the Decameron.
ev.eur_h_black_death.flee.success: In a remote village the plague did not find you.
ev.eur_h_black_death.care: Stay and care for the sick
ev.eur_h_black_death.care.success: You buried the dead and fed the sick – and by some miracle did not fall ill.
ev.eur_h_black_death.care.failure: You fell ill. The people you nursed are now nursing you.
ev.eur_h_black_death.pray: Pray and walk in the procession
ev.eur_h_black_death.pray.success: The plague passed your house by.
ev.eur_h_black_death.pray.failure: In the crowd of the procession you caught the sickness.
ev.eur_h_flagellants.title: The flagellants
ev.eur_h_flagellants.text: A procession of penitents has entered the city: hundreds of men in white sing hymns and scourge themselves to turn aside God's wrath. The crowd weeps and reaches toward them. Some of them shout that the Jews are to blame.
ev.eur_h_flagellants.note: The flagellant movement swept Germany and the Low Countries in 1348–1349. Their processions were often accompanied by pogroms. In October 1349 Pope Clement VI condemned the movement.
ev.eur_h_flagellants.shun: Turn away: God does not want blood
ev.eur_h_pogrom_1349.title: A night in August
ev.eur_h_pogrom_1349.text: A rumour is creeping through the city that the Jews poisoned the wells and brought the plague. The council hesitates, and a crowd is gathering at the Jewish quarter. Tonight something terrible may happen.
ev.eur_h_pogrom_1349.note: On the night of 23–24 August 1349 a mob attacked the Jewish quarter of Cologne; the community was almost entirely destroyed. Similar massacres during the Black Death swept dozens of German towns.
ev.eur_h_pogrom_1349.hide.success: You survived the night in an acquaintance's cellar. The quarter is gone.
ev.eur_h_pogrom_1349.hide.failure: They found you. You survived by a miracle, having lost everything.
ev.eur_h_jacquerie.title: The Jacquerie
ev.eur_h_jacquerie.text: The king is a prisoner of the English, the lords squeeze taxes for his ransom, and mercenaries plunder the villages. The peasants of the Beauvaisis have taken up scythes and are burning castles. In Paris the merchant provost Étienne Marcel defies the Dauphin.
ev.eur_h_jacquerie.note: The Jacquerie was a peasant revolt in northern France in May–June 1358. It was brutally crushed after the fighting at Meaux and Clermont. In the same year Étienne Marcel was killed in Paris.
ev.eur_h_jacquerie.join.success: You got home while the knights scoured the neighbouring villages. No one informed on you.
ev.eur_h_jacquerie.join.failure: At Meaux the knights scattered the rebels. You survived, but your village was burned.
ev.eur_h_jacquerie.hide: Wait it out in the woods
ev.eur_h_jacquerie.lords: Take up arms with the lords
ev.eur_h_ciompi.title: The Ciompi
ev.eur_h_ciompi.text: The wool carders and day labourers, who have no guild of their own, have seized the Palazzo della Signoria. Their leader, the carder Michele di Lando, has become Gonfalonier. The city holds its breath.
ev.eur_h_ciompi.note: The Ciompi revolt of July 1378 was a rising of the hired workers of Florence's cloth industry. They won guilds of their own, but in 1382 the old guilds regained power.
ev.eur_h_ciompi.join.success: For a while you have your own guild and a voice. That has never happened before.
ev.eur_h_ciompi.join.failure: The revolt ran out of steam, and the masters remembered who was in the crowd.
ev.eur_h_ciompi.defend: Board up the shop and wait
ev.eur_h_schism.title: Two popes
ev.eur_h_schism.text: The cardinals have elected two popes at once: one sits in Rome, the other in Avignon, and each excommunicates the other and his followers. Whom are you to believe now?
ev.eur_h_schism.text.paris: The cardinals have elected two popes at once. Our king recognises the Pope in Avignon, the English the one in Rome. Each excommunicates the other. Whom are you to believe now?
ev.eur_h_schism.text.london: The cardinals have elected two popes at once. England stands by Pope Urban in Rome, the French by the one in Avignon. Each excommunicates the other. Whom are you to believe now?
ev.eur_h_schism.text.toledo: The cardinals have elected two popes at once, and after long debate Castile has recognised the one in Avignon. Each excommunicates the other. Whom are you to believe now?
ev.eur_h_schism.note: The Great Western Schism (1378–1417): after Urban VI was elected, some cardinals chose Clement VII, who settled in Avignon. France, Scotland and Castile backed Avignon, England and most of the Empire backed Rome. The schism ended at the Council of Constance.
ev.eur_h_peasants_revolt.title: When Adam delved
ev.eur_h_peasants_revolt.text: The poll tax was the last straw. The peasants of Kent and Essex under Wat Tyler have entered London. The priest John Ball cries: "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?" The Savoy palace is burning.
ev.eur_h_peasants_revolt.note: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was sparked by the third poll tax. On 15 June at Smithfield Wat Tyler was killed while parleying with the fourteen-year-old King Richard II. The king did not keep his promises to abolish serfdom.
ev.eur_h_peasants_revolt.join.success: You stood at Smithfield when the king promised freedom. The promise was broken, but you came home alive.
ev.eur_h_peasants_revolt.join.failure: After Tyler was killed the reprisals began. You did not escape them.
ev.eur_h_peasants_revolt.guard: Guard the gates with the city watch
ev.eur_h_toledo_1391.title: The summer of 1391
ev.eur_h_toledo_1391.text: A wave of riots is spreading from Seville. A mob roused by an archdeacon's sermons has burst into the Jewish quarter of Toledo. Neighbours are knocking at Christian doors begging for shelter.
ev.eur_h_toledo_1391.text.judaism: A wave of riots is spreading from Seville. A mob has burst into the Jewish quarter of Toledo, and the synagogues are burning. You knock at the doors of Christians you know.
ev.eur_h_toledo_1391.text.islam: A wave of riots is spreading from Seville. A mob has burst into the Jewish quarter of Toledo. Jewish neighbours are knocking at your door begging for shelter.
ev.eur_h_toledo_1391.note: The riots of 1391 began in Seville on 6 June and swept through Castile and Aragon; in Toledo the quarter was sacked on 18 June. Thousands died and tens of thousands were forcibly baptised – the origin of the "New Christians", the conversos.
ev.eur_h_toledo_1391.shelter.success: You hid people for three days. Everyone survived.
ev.eur_h_toledo_1391.shelter.failure: The mob found out and broke down your door. You were hurt, but the people got away.
ev.eur_h_france_1394.title: Exile again
ev.eur_h_france_1394.text: King Charles has ordered the Jews expelled from the kingdom – this time for good. A life barely rebuilt is packed into bundles once more.
ev.eur_h_france_1394.note: On 17 September 1394 Charles VI decreed the expulsion of the Jews from the Kingdom of France. Afterwards Jewish communities survived only in lands outside the king's rule – Provence, Alsace, papal Avignon.
ev.eur_h_agincourt.title: Agincourt
ev.eur_h_agincourt.text: At Agincourt a small English army destroyed a huge French one.
ev.eur_h_agincourt.text.paris: At Agincourt the French knights bogged down in the autumn mud under English arrows. Dukes, the Constable and hundreds of nobles were killed. Paris is in mourning, and the Burgundians and Armagnacs blame one another.
ev.eur_h_agincourt.text.london: King Henry has come back from France victorious: at Agincourt a handful of hungry Englishmen destroyed a whole army. London welcomes him with a triumph and songs.
ev.eur_h_agincourt.note: On 25 October 1415 Henry V's army routed the French at Agincourt. Five years later, by the Treaty of Troyes, Henry was recognised as heir to the French crown.
ev.eur_h_cologne_1424.title: The council refuses
ev.eur_h_cologne_1424.text: The city council has announced that the Jews' right to live in Cologne will not be renewed. By autumn the quarter must be empty, and the synagogue will be turned into a chapel.
ev.eur_h_cologne_1424.note: In 1424 the Cologne council refused to renew the Jews' right of residence, and the community was expelled. The synagogue was rebuilt as the council chapel. Jews returned to Cologne only at the end of the eighteenth century.
ev.eur_h_joan.title: The Maid
ev.eur_h_joan.text: They say a peasant girl from Lorraine, who heard the voices of saints, raised the siege of Orléans and led the Dauphin to his coronation at Reims.
ev.eur_h_joan.text.paris: Paris is held by the English and Burgundians, and under the walls stands the Dauphin's army with a girl in armour riding at its head – Joan. She was wounded at the Saint-Honoré gate, and the assault was beaten off. Who is she – saint or witch?
ev.eur_h_joan.text.london: Strange news comes from France: some peasant girl in armour leads the French into battle and beats our captains. In London they say it is witchcraft.
ev.eur_h_joan.note: Joan of Arc raised the siege of Orléans in May 1429, and in July Charles VII was crowned at Reims. In September 1429 the assault on Paris failed. Captured by the Burgundians, she was condemned by a church court and burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431.
ev.eur_h_medici.title: Cosimo returns
ev.eur_h_medici.text: A year ago the banker Cosimo de' Medici was exiled, and now a new Signoria calls him back. The people greet him at the gates, and his enemies the Albizzi go into exile themselves. It is clear who will rule the city now – without a title, through his friends.
ev.eur_h_medici.note: Cosimo de' Medici was exiled in 1433 and returned in triumph in the autumn of 1434. From then on the Medici effectively ruled Florence while keeping the outward forms of the republic.
ev.eur_h_medici.albizzi.success: The Medici forgave you and even invited you into business.
ev.eur_h_medici.albizzi.failure: Your name turned up on the lists of the unreliable. Your taxes suddenly rose.
ev.eur_h_dome.title: The dome
ev.eur_h_dome.text: The Pope has consecrated the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore. Over the city rises Brunelleschi's dome – built without centring, without supports, the like of which has not been raised since the Romans. The whole city stands with heads tipped back.
ev.eur_h_dome.note: Santa Maria del Fiore was consecrated by Pope Eugene IV on 25 March 1436. Filippo Brunelleschi's dome, built from 1420, was the largest in the world.
ev.eur_h_hanse.title: The Confederation of Cologne
ev.eur_h_hanse.text: Envoys of the Hanseatic towns, from Lübeck to Amsterdam, have gathered in Cologne's town hall. They have resolved to make war on the Danish king, who strangles trade with tolls in the Sound. The merchants are clubbing together for ships.
ev.eur_h_hanse.note: In November 1367 Hanseatic and Dutch towns formed an alliance at Cologne against Valdemar IV of Denmark. Victory was sealed by the Peace of Stralsund in 1370 – the height of the Hanseatic League's power.
ev.eur_h_hanse.invest: Invest in fitting out the ships
ev.eur_h_hanse.invest.success: The Danes gave way and the tolls were lifted. Your share came back with a profit.
ev.eur_h_hanse.invest.failure: The ship carrying your share ran aground off Scania.
ev.eur_h_hanse.watch: Watch the envoys at the town hall
ev.eur_h_printing.title: The printing press
ev.eur_h_printing.text: A master from the Rhine has set up a printing press in town: lead letters, a press like a wine press – and in a day as many pages as a monk copies in half a year.
ev.eur_h_printing.text.cologne: Ulrich Zell, who learned the craft at Mainz, has set up a press in Cologne. In a day it makes as many pages as a monk copies in half a year.
ev.eur_h_printing.text.paris: In a cellar of the Sorbonne German craftsmen have set up a printing press. The masters argue whether it is a blessing or ruin for the copyists.
ev.eur_h_printing.text.london: The merchant William Caxton has come back from Bruges and opened a shop by Westminster under the sign of the red pale: he prints books in English.
ev.eur_h_printing.note: Johannes Gutenberg began printing with movable type at Mainz around 1450. Ulrich Zell opened a press in Cologne in 1465; a press began work in Paris in 1470, in Florence in 1471, and Caxton's at Westminster in 1476.
ev.eur_h_printing.scoff: A manuscript is a real book
ev.eur_h_wars_roses.title: The White Rose and the Red
ev.eur_h_wars_roses.text: York and Lancaster are fighting over the crown again. The king is one day a prisoner, the next back on the throne, and the Londoners shut the gates first against one army, then another.
ev.eur_h_wars_roses.note: The Wars of the Roses (1455–1487) were the struggle of Lancaster and York for the English throne: the battles of St Albans (1455), Towton (1461), Barnet and Tewkesbury (1471), and Bosworth (1485).
ev.eur_h_pazzi.title: The Pazzi conspiracy
ev.eur_h_pazzi.text: At Easter Mass in the cathedral conspirators of the Pazzi family fell upon the Medici brothers. Giuliano was killed, Lorenzo wounded but saved. By evening the city had dealt with the conspirators.
ev.eur_h_pazzi.note: The Pazzi conspiracy of 26 April 1478 had the backing of Pope Sixtus IV. Giuliano de' Medici was killed, Lorenzo survived. The conspirators, including the Archbishop of Pisa, were hanged, and war with the Pope and Naples followed.
ev.eur_h_toledo_1449.title: The Sentence-Statute
ev.eur_h_toledo_1449.text: The townsfolk have risen against a new tax and sacked the houses of rich conversos, and the rebel council has decreed that descendants of baptised Jews may not hold city office. People speak of "purity of blood".
ev.eur_h_toledo_1449.note: In 1449 a revolt in Toledo led by Pero Sarmiento produced the "Sentence-Statute", the first "purity of blood" statute, barring conversos from office. The Pope condemned it, but similar statutes spread across Spain.
ev.eur_h_toledo_1449.protest: Say that the baptised are Christians
ev.eur_h_toledo_1449.protest.success: Many agree with you – quietly, but they agree.
ev.eur_h_toledo_1449.protest.failure: You yourself came under suspicion of "impure blood".
ev.eur_h_granada.title: Granada has fallen
ev.eur_h_granada.text: The last emir of Granada has handed the keys of the Alhambra to Ferdinand and Isabella. In Toledo every bell is ringing: after nearly eight hundred years the whole peninsula is Christian again.
ev.eur_h_granada.text.islam: The last emir of Granada has handed the keys of the Alhambra to Ferdinand and Isabella. Toledo's bells ring all day, but in the Moorish quarter it is quiet: the last Muslim kingdom of the peninsula is gone.
ev.eur_h_granada.note: On 2 January 1492 Muhammad XII surrendered Granada to the Catholic Monarchs, completing the Reconquista. That same year Columbus sailed west and reached America.
ev.eur_h_spain_expulsion.title: The Alhambra Decree
ev.eur_h_spain_expulsion.text: The monarchs have decreed that by the end of July every Jew who has not been baptised must leave Castile and Aragon. No gold or silver may be taken. Houses sell for a donkey, a vineyard for a length of cloth.
ev.eur_h_spain_expulsion.note: The Alhambra Decree was signed on 31 March 1492. Tens of thousands of Jews left for Portugal, Navarre, Italy, North Africa and the Ottoman Empire; many were baptised in order to stay.
ev.eur_h_savonarola.title: The bonfire of the vanities
ev.eur_h_savonarola.text: The Medici have been driven out, and the friar Savonarola thunders from the pulpit of coming punishment. Bands of boys go from house to house collecting mirrors, playing cards, lutes, fine dresses and books – for a huge bonfire in the Piazza della Signoria.
ev.eur_h_savonarola.note: In 1494, after Charles VIII's invasion, the Medici fled and the Dominican Girolamo Savonarola rose to power in the city. The "bonfire of the vanities" took place in February 1497. In May 1498 Savonarola was executed in the same square.
ev.eur_h_savonarola.burn: Give up your "vanities" to the fire
ev.eur_h_savonarola.hide.failure: You were named from the pulpit as "a secret sinner".
ev.eur_h_savonarola.mock.success: Many laugh with you in secret. A year later the whole city will be laughing.
ev.eur_h_savonarola.mock.failure: The friar's followers pelted you with stones.
